questions.topic: Unit 3 (Crop Production): Soil, Soil Fertility, Fertilizers and Manures
questions.sub_topic: Nitrogen supplied with a phosphorus dose from DAP
questions.question: A farmer supplies 46 kg P₂O₅ per hectare using DAP (18-46-0) alone. How much nitrogen does this add at the same time?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) 18 kg
Why: Step 1: DAP has 46% P₂O₅, so 100 kg DAP supplies 46 kg P₂O₅.
Step 2: the farmer therefore applies 100 kg DAP.
Step 3: DAP has 18% N, so 100 kg DAP adds 18 kg N.
Why not the others:
(B) 23 kg is half of 46, which is not how the grade works.
(C) 36 kg would need 200 kg DAP.
(D) 46 kg confuses the P₂O₅ figure with N.
Key point: Find the fertilizer quantity from one nutrient, then read the others off its grade.

questions.topic: Unit 2 (Livestock Production): Livestock: Care, Management and Diseases
questions.sub_topic: Animal diseases and their typical signs
questions.question:
Match List-I (Disease) with List-II (Typical sign).

List-I
(A) Haemorrhagic septicaemia
(B) Mastitis
(C) Fowl pox
(D) Ranikhet disease

List-II
(I) Wart-like scabs on the comb and wattles
(II) Twisted neck, gasping and greenish diarrhoea in birds
(III) Clots and flakes in milk with a swollen udder
(IV) High fever with a hot, painful swelling of the throat
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) (A)-(IV), (B)-(III), (C)-(I), (D)-(II)
Why: HS causes high fever and a hot swelling of the throat (IV). Mastitis causes clots in milk and a swollen udder (III). Fowl pox causes wart-like scabs on the comb (I). Ranikhet disease causes nervous signs such as a twisted neck, gasping and greenish diarrhoea (II).
Why not the others: Option (A) swaps HS and mastitis. Option (B) swaps mastitis and fowl pox. Option (D) swaps fowl pox and Ranikhet.
Key point: Learn one sign that marks each disease.

questions.topic: Unit 1 (Agrometeorology, Genetics and Plant Breeding, Biochemistry and Microbiology): Agrometeorology
questions.sub_topic: Months of the southwest monsoon season
questions.question: The southwest monsoon season in India covers the months of:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) June to September
Why: The southwest monsoon season runs from June to September and brings most of India's annual rainfall.
Why not the others:
(B) October–December is the post-monsoon (northeast monsoon) season.
(C) January–February is winter.
(D) March–May is the hot pre-monsoon season.
Key point: SW monsoon: June–September.

questions.topic: Unit 3 (Crop Production): Irrigation and Drainage
questions.sub_topic: Largest source of irrigation in India
questions.question: Which source irrigates the largest share of India's net irrigated area?
options: C) Tube wells and other wells
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Tube wells and other wells
Why: Groundwater from tube wells and other wells irrigates over 60% of the net irrigated area.
Why not the others: (A) canals, (B) tanks and (D) lift schemes have smaller shares.
Key point: India irrigates mostly from groundwater, which is why water tables are falling.

questions.topic: Unit 4 (Horticulture): Horticulture: Importance, Orchards, Gardens and Propagation
questions.sub_topic: Orchard layout systems
questions.question:
Match List-I (Layout system) with List-II (Description).

List-I
(A) Square system
(B) Rectangular system
(C) Triangular (hexagonal) system
(D) Contour system

List-II
(I) Plants at the corners of squares, equally spaced in both directions
(II) Planting along lines of equal elevation on sloping land
(III) Spacing between rows wider than spacing within a row
(IV) Plants at the corners of equilateral triangles, fitting about 15% more plants
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) (A)-(I), (B)-(III), (C)-(IV), (D)-(II)
Why: In the square system plants are equally spaced both ways (I). The rectangular system has wider rows than plant spacing (III). The triangular (hexagonal) system sets plants at the corners of equilateral triangles and fits about 15% more plants (IV). The contour system follows lines of equal elevation on slopes (II).
Why not the others: Option (A) swaps square and rectangular. Option (B) swaps rectangular and triangular. Option (C) swaps triangular and contour.
Key point: Hexagonal fits most plants; contour suits slopes.

questions.topic: Unit 1 (Agrometeorology, Genetics and Plant Breeding, Biochemistry and Microbiology): Biochemistry
questions.sub_topic: Why strong heat stops an enzyme
questions.question: Why does an enzyme stop working when it is heated strongly?
options: A) Because heat changes the shape of the protein, destroying its active site
B) Because heat turns the enzyme protein into a simple carbohydrate
C) Because heat increases the amount of substrate far too much for it
D) Because heat makes the enzyme dissolve and wash out of the cell
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Because heat changes the shape of the protein, destroying its active site
Why: Enzymes are proteins. High temperature breaks the bonds that hold their shape (denaturation), so the active site no longer fits the substrate.
Why not the others:
(B) Heat does not change a protein into a carbohydrate.
(C) Heat does not create substrate.
(D) Dissolving faster would not stop activity.
Key point: Heat denatures enzymes; each has an optimum temperature.

questions.topic: Unit 4 (Horticulture): Fruit and Vegetable Preservation
questions.sub_topic: Methods of preservation — which hold
questions.question:
Consider the following statements:
(A) Drying preserves food by lowering the water available to microbes.
(B) Salt preserves pickles by drawing water out of food and microbes.
(C) Irradiation is a method of food preservation.
(D) Canning combines heat processing with an airtight seal.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) (A), (B), (C) and (D)
Why: All four are true. Drying and salting reduce available water, irradiation kills or inactivates microbes, and canning kills microbes with heat and keeps new ones out with a seal.
Why not the others: Options (A), (B) and (D) each leave out at least one true statement.
Key point: Preservation removes, inhibits or kills microbes and keeps them out.

questions.topic: Unit 2 (Livestock Production): Artificial Insemination and Livestock Products
questions.sub_topic: Starting material for ghee
questions.question: Ghee is made by heating ________ to drive off its moisture.
options: C) the whey left after curdling
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) butter or cream
Why: Butter or cream is heated until almost all the water evaporates, leaving clarified butterfat (ghee).
Why not the others:
(B) Paneer is a coagulated protein product.
(C) Whey is the liquid left after curdling and has little fat.
(D) Khoa is concentrated whole milk.
Key point: Butter → heat → ghee.

questions.topic: Unit 3 (Crop Production): Weed Control
questions.sub_topic: Order of herbicide application times
questions.question:
Arrange the following times of herbicide application in the order in which they occur in a crop season.
(A) Late post-emergence
(B) Pre-plant incorporation
(C) Early post-emergence
(D) Pre-emergence
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) (B), (D), (C), (A)
Why: Pre-plant incorporation (B) is done before sowing. Pre-emergence (D) is after sowing but before the weeds and crop emerge. Early post-emergence (C) is soon after emergence, and late post-emergence (A) comes later.
Why not the others: Option (A) puts pre-emergence before pre-plant. Option (B) puts early post-emergence before pre-emergence. Option (C) puts late before early post-emergence.
Key point: Pre-plant → pre-emergence → early post → late post.

questions.topic: Unit 4 (Horticulture): Cultivation of Fruits, Vegetables and Flowers
questions.sub_topic: Usual planting material of marigold
questions.question: Marigold is usually propagated by:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) seed
Why: Marigold is an annual raised from seed, sown in a nursery and transplanted.
Why not the others:
(B) Corms are used for gladiolus.
(C) Rhizomes are used for canna.
(D) Budding is used for roses.
Key point: Marigold — seed; gladiolus — corms; canna — rhizomes.

questions.topic: Unit 1 (Agrometeorology, Genetics and Plant Breeding, Biochemistry and Microbiology): Microbiology
questions.sub_topic: Use of Trichoderma in crop protection
questions.question: *Trichoderma*, a fungus applied to seed or soil, is used in agriculture mainly as a:
options: A) nitrogen-fixing biofertilizer for legume crops like gram
B) biocontrol agent against soil-borne plant pathogens
C) source of the meat-tenderising enzyme papain
D) yeast for fermenting fruit juice into wine
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) biocontrol agent against soil-borne plant pathogens
Why: *Trichoderma* species attack and outcompete soil-borne fungi such as *Fusarium*, *Rhizoctonia* and *Pythium*.
Why not the others:
(A) It does not fix nitrogen.
(C) Papain comes from papaya latex.
(D) It is not a yeast.
Key point: *Trichoderma* is a friendly fungus that fights root and wilt diseases.

questions.topic: Unit 3 (Crop Production): Soil, Soil Fertility, Fertilizers and Manures
questions.sub_topic: Essential nutrients — which statement is wrong
questions.question:
Consider the following statements about essential plant nutrients:
(A) Carbon, hydrogen and oxygen are obtained from air and water.
(B) Calcium, magnesium and sulphur are secondary nutrients.
(C) Iron and zinc are needed in large amounts, so they are macronutrients.
(D) Nickel is recognised as an essential micronutrient.
Which of the statements given above is NOT correct?
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) (C) only
Why: (C) is false: iron and zinc are needed in very small amounts and are micronutrients. (A), (B) and (D) are correct.
Why not the others: Statements (A), (B) and (D) are all correct.
Key point: Primary NPK, secondary Ca–Mg–S, micronutrients such as Fe, Zn, Cu, Mn, B, Mo, Cl and Ni.

questions.topic: Unit 2 (Livestock Production): Artificial Insemination and Livestock Products
questions.sub_topic: Main sugar in milk
questions.question: The main carbohydrate (sugar) present in milk is:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) lactose
Why: Lactose, made of glucose and galactose, is the natural sugar of milk, at about 4.5–5%.
Why not the others:
(A) Sucrose is cane sugar.
(B) Maltose comes from starch.
(D) Fructose is fruit sugar.
Key point: Milk sugar = lactose.

questions.topic: Unit 2 (Livestock Production): Livestock: Scope, Importance and Breeds
questions.sub_topic: Dairy development — which statements hold
questions.question:
Consider the following statements:
(A) The National Dairy Development Board was set up in 1965 with its headquarters at Anand.
(B) Amul is the brand of a dairy cooperative in Gujarat.
(C) Operation Flood aimed mainly at importing milk powder permanently.
(D) The White Revolution refers to a rapid rise in egg production.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) (A) and (B) only
Why: (A) and (B) are true. (C) is false: Operation Flood used gifted milk powder only at first, to raise money to build India's own dairy capacity. (D) is false: the White Revolution refers to milk.
Why not the others: Options (B), (C) and (D) all include at least one false statement.
Key point: NDDB at Anand (1965); Amul; the White Revolution is about milk.

questions.topic: Unit 1 (Agrometeorology, Genetics and Plant Breeding, Biochemistry and Microbiology): Microbiology
questions.sub_topic: Order of nitrogen transformations in soil
questions.question:
Arrange the forms of nitrogen in the order in which microbes convert them in the soil.
(A) Nitrite (NO₂⁻)
(B) Organic nitrogen in residues
(C) Nitrate (NO₃⁻)
(D) Ammonium (NH₄⁺)
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) (B), (D), (A), (C)
Why: Organic nitrogen (B) is broken down to ammonium (D) by ammonification. *Nitrosomonas* oxidises ammonium to nitrite (A), and *Nitrobacter* oxidises nitrite to nitrate (C).
Why not the others: Option (A) puts nitrite before ammonium. Option (C) starts with ammonium. Option (D) puts nitrate before nitrite.
Key point: Organic N → NH₄⁺ → NO₂⁻ → NO₃⁻.

questions.topic: Unit 2 (Livestock Production): Livestock: Care, Management and Diseases
questions.sub_topic: Disease prevented by the Lasota vaccine
questions.question: The F1 and Lasota vaccines, given to young chicks as eye or nasal drops, protect against:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Ranikhet disease
Why: F1 and Lasota are live vaccines against Ranikhet (Newcastle) disease, given to chicks in their first weeks.
Why not the others:
(A) Coccidiosis is controlled with coccidiostats and dry litter.
(C) Fowl pox has its own vaccine, given by wing-web stab.
(D) Mastitis affects milch animals.
Key point: Ranikhet — F1/Lasota by eye or nose drop.

questions.topic: Unit 2 (Livestock Production): Fisheries
questions.sub_topic: What the Blue Revolution refers to
questions.question: The 'Blue Revolution' in India refers to rapid growth in:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) fish production
Why: The Blue Revolution is the rapid growth of fisheries and aquaculture.
Why not the others:
(A) Milk is the White Revolution.
(B) Oilseeds are the Yellow Revolution.
(C) Eggs are part of the Silver Revolution.
Key point: Blue — fish; white — milk; yellow — oilseeds.

questions.topic: Unit 3 (Crop Production): Field Crops: Cultivation, Protection and Post-harvest
questions.sub_topic: Why gram is nipped
questions.question: Why do farmers nip (pinch off) the growing tips of gram plants at about 30–40 days?
options: A) To encourage branching, which gives more flowers and pods
B) To kill the pod borer eggs laid on the growing tips
C) To stop the plant from flowering too early in the season
D) To reduce the plant's need for irrigation water later
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) To encourage branching, which gives more flowers and pods
Why: Nipping removes apical dominance, so the plant branches more and bears more flowers and pods. The tender tips can also be eaten as a green vegetable.
Why not the others:
(B) Nipping is not a pest control method.
(C) Its purpose is more branches, not delayed flowering.
(D) It does not change water need much.
Key point: Nip gram for more branches and pods.

questions.topic: Unit 4 (Horticulture): Fruit and Vegetable Preservation
questions.sub_topic: Minimum fruit juice in a squash
questions.question: Under Indian food standards, a fruit squash must contain at least about ________ fruit juice.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) 25 percent
Why: A squash must contain at least 25% fruit juice, with about 40% or more total soluble solids, and is diluted before drinking.
Why not the others:
(A) 5% is closer to a cordial or drink.
(C) and (D) are typical of juices or nectars, not squash.
Key point: Squash: at least 25% juice and about 40% TSS.

questions.topic: Unit 3 (Crop Production): Field Crops: Cultivation, Protection and Post-harvest
questions.sub_topic: Where groundnut pods develop
questions.question: In groundnut, the pods develop:
options: A) in clusters on the main stem above ground
B) inside the flower on the plant
C) underground, after the peg pushes into the soil
D) at the tips of the roots like tubers
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) underground, after the peg pushes into the soil
Why: After fertilisation the ovary stalk (peg or gynophore) grows down into the soil, where the pod forms. This is why groundnut needs loose, friable soil.
Why not the others:
(A) and (B) The pods do not form above ground.
(D) They are not root tubers.
Key point: Groundnut flowers above ground and fruits below it.

questions.topic: Unit 4 (Horticulture): Horticulture: Importance, Orchards, Gardens and Propagation
questions.sub_topic: Order of steps in T-budding
questions.question:
Arrange the steps of T-budding in the correct order.
(A) Wrap the bud union with a polythene strip
(B) Insert the bud shield under the bark flaps
(C) Lift the flaps of bark
(D) Make a T-shaped cut on the rootstock
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) (D), (C), (B), (A)
Why: A T-shaped cut is made on the rootstock (D), its bark flaps are lifted (C), the bud shield is slipped under them (B), and the union is wrapped tightly with polythene (A).
Why not the others: Option (A) inserts the bud before lifting the flaps. Option (C) lifts flaps before making the cut. Option (D) wraps before inserting the bud.
Key point: Cut → lift → insert → wrap.

questions.topic: Unit 1 (Agrometeorology, Genetics and Plant Breeding, Biochemistry and Microbiology): Seed Science
questions.sub_topic: Seed formation without fertilisation
questions.question: The formation of seed without fertilisation, which can fix hybrid vigour, is called:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) apomixis
Why: In apomixis, an embryo develops without the fusion of gametes, so the seed is a clone of the mother plant.
Why not the others:
(B) Parthenocarpy produces seedless fruit, not seed.
(C) Polyembryony is the presence of more than one embryo in a seed.
(D) Vernalization is cold treatment to induce flowering.
Key point: Apomixis = seed without sex.

questions.topic: Unit 2 (Livestock Production): Livestock: Care, Management and Diseases
questions.sub_topic: Feed that is not a roughage
questions.question: Roughages are bulky, fibrous feeds. Which one of the following feeds does NOT fall in this group?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Groundnut cake
Why: Groundnut cake is a concentrate: low in fibre and rich in protein.
Why not the others: (A) wheat straw, (B) berseem and (C) maize silage are bulky, fibrous roughages.
Key point: Roughages are bulky and fibrous; concentrates are dense in nutrients.

questions.topic: Unit 1 (Agrometeorology, Genetics and Plant Breeding, Biochemistry and Microbiology): Agrometeorology
questions.sub_topic: Why terminal heat cuts wheat yield
questions.question: Why does a spell of high temperature during grain filling (terminal heat) reduce the yield of wheat?
options: A) Because heat makes the plants produce many more late tillers
B) Because it shortens the grain-filling period, so grains stay small
C) Because heat kills the root nodules that supply the crop nitrogen
D) Because heat delays flowering by several weeks in most varieties
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Because it shortens the grain-filling period, so grains stay small
Why: High temperature speeds up development, so the grain-filling period is cut short and the grains are shrivelled and light.
Why not the others:
(A) Late heat does not raise tiller number.
(C) Wheat has no root nodules.
(D) At grain filling, flowering is already over.
Key point: Terminal heat means lighter grains; warming climates make it more common.

questions.topic: Unit 3 (Crop Production): Soil, Soil Fertility, Fertilizers and Manures
questions.sub_topic: Soil pH suitable for most crops
questions.question: Most field crops grow best when soil pH is about:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) 6.5–7.5
Why: Near-neutral soil (pH 6.5–7.5) keeps most nutrients available and suits most soil microbes.
Why not the others:
(A) Strongly acid soils cause aluminium toxicity and P fixation.
(C) and (D) Strongly alkaline soils lock up micronutrients and may be sodic.
Key point: Near-neutral pH suits most crops.

questions.topic: Unit 3 (Crop Production): Irrigation and Drainage
questions.sub_topic: Scheduling irrigation — which statement is wrong
questions.question:
Consider the following statements about scheduling irrigation:
(A) Irrigation can be scheduled by the critical growth stages of a crop.
(B) Irrigation should be given only after the plants have reached the permanent wilting point.
(C) The IW/CPE ratio is a climatological approach to scheduling.
(D) Irrigation can be given when a set fraction, such as half, of the available soil moisture is used up.
Which of the statements given above is NOT correct?
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) (B) only
Why: (B) is false: at the permanent wilting point plants cannot recover, so irrigation must come well before it. (A), (C) and (D) are accepted approaches.
Why not the others: Statements (A), (C) and (D) are all correct.
Key point: Irrigate before stress becomes damage.

questions.topic: Unit 3 (Crop Production): Irrigation and Drainage
questions.sub_topic: Order of irrigation methods by efficiency
questions.question:
Arrange the following irrigation methods from the highest to the lowest water application efficiency.
(A) Sprinkler
(B) Wild flooding
(C) Drip
(D) Furrow
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) (C), (A), (D), (B)
Why: Drip (C) is the most efficient, at about 90%. Sprinkler (A) follows at about 75–80%. Furrow (D) is a controlled surface method at about 50–60%. Wild flooding (B) is the least efficient.
Why not the others: Option (A) puts sprinkler above drip. Option (B) puts furrow above sprinkler. Option (D) puts wild flooding above furrow.
Key point: Drip > sprinkler > furrow > flooding.

questions.topic: Unit 3 (Crop Production): Crop Production: Introduction and Modern Agriculture
questions.sub_topic: A cereal crop
questions.question: Cereals are grasses grown for their edible grain. Which one of these crops is a cereal?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Sorghum
Why: Sorghum (jowar) is a cereal: a grass grown for its grain.
Why not the others:
(A) Groundnut and (B) mustard are oilseeds.
(D) Chickpea is a pulse.
Key point: Cereals are grasses grown for grain.

questions.topic: Unit 3 (Crop Production): Field Crops: Cultivation, Protection and Post-harvest
questions.sub_topic: Insect pests and the crops they attack
questions.question:
Match List-I (Pest) with List-II (Crop it chiefly attacks).

List-I
(A) Yellow stem borer
(B) Pod borer (*Helicoverpa armigera*)
(C) Aphid (*Lipaphis erysimi*)
(D) Early shoot borer

List-II
(I) Sugarcane
(II) Rice
(III) Mustard
(IV) Chickpea
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) (A)-(II), (B)-(IV), (C)-(III), (D)-(I)
Why: The yellow stem borer attacks rice (II), causing dead hearts and white ears. *Helicoverpa* bores into chickpea pods (IV). *Lipaphis* is the mustard aphid (III). The early shoot borer attacks young sugarcane (I).
Why not the others: Option (B) swaps stem borer and pod borer. Option (C) swaps pod borer and aphid. Option (D) swaps aphid and shoot borer.
Key point: Learn the key pest of each major crop.

questions.topic: Unit 1 (Agrometeorology, Genetics and Plant Breeding, Biochemistry and Microbiology): Agrometeorology
questions.sub_topic: Greenhouse gases and their major sources
questions.question:
Match List-I (Greenhouse gas) with List-II (A major source).

List-I
(A) Carbon dioxide
(B) Methane
(C) Nitrous oxide
(D) Chlorofluorocarbons

List-II
(I) Refrigerants and aerosol sprays
(II) Nitrogen fertilizers applied to soils
(III) Enteric fermentation in ruminant animals
(IV) Burning of fossil fuels and deforestation
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) (A)-(IV), (B)-(III), (C)-(II), (D)-(I)
Why: CO₂ comes mainly from fossil fuels and deforestation (IV). Methane comes from ruminant digestion and flooded rice (III). Nitrous oxide comes from nitrogen fertilizers in soil (II). CFCs come from refrigerants and sprays (I).
Why not the others: Option (A) swaps CO₂ and methane. Option (B) swaps methane and nitrous oxide. Option (D) swaps nitrous oxide and CFCs.
Key point: Agriculture is a major source of methane and nitrous oxide.

questions.topic: Unit 4 (Horticulture): Cultivation of Fruits, Vegetables and Flowers
questions.sub_topic: Cause of whiptail in cauliflower
questions.question: 'Whiptail' in cauliflower, where leaf blades are narrow and strap-like, is caused by a deficiency of:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) molybdenum
Why: Whiptail is caused by molybdenum deficiency, especially in acid soils; liming and sodium molybdate correct it.
Why not the others:
(A) Boron deficiency causes browning of the curd.
(B) Nitrogen shortage contributes to buttoning.
(C) Manganese deficiency causes interveinal chlorosis and grey specks.
Key point: Whiptail — molybdenum.

questions.topic: Unit 2 (Livestock Production): Livestock: Care, Management and Diseases
questions.sub_topic: Disease eradicated worldwide
questions.question: Which cattle disease was declared eradicated from the whole world in 2011?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Rinderpest
Why: Rinderpest (cattle plague) was declared eradicated globally in 2011; India had become free of it earlier.
Why not the others: (B) FMD, (C) BQ and (D) HS still occur and are controlled by vaccination.
Key point: Rinderpest is the only animal disease eradicated worldwide so far.

questions.topic: Unit 4 (Horticulture): Cultivation of Fruits, Vegetables and Flowers
questions.sub_topic: Not a grape variety
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a variety of grape?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Dashehari
Why: Dashehari is a mango variety of Uttar Pradesh.
Why not the others: (A) Thompson Seedless, (B) Anab-e-Shahi and (C) Perlette are grape varieties.
Key point: Dashehari is a mango; Thompson Seedless is a grape.

questions.topic: Unit 1 (Agrometeorology, Genetics and Plant Breeding, Biochemistry and Microbiology): Biochemistry
questions.sub_topic: Bond joining amino acids in proteins
questions.question: In a protein, amino acids are joined to one another by:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) peptide bonds
Why: The amino group of one amino acid joins the carboxyl group of the next, forming a peptide bond.
Why not the others:
(A) Glycosidic bonds join sugars.
(B) Ester bonds join glycerol and fatty acids.
(D) Phosphodiester bonds join nucleotides.
Key point: Proteins — peptide bonds; carbohydrates — glycosidic bonds.

questions.topic: Unit 3 (Crop Production): Crop Production: Introduction and Modern Agriculture
questions.sub_topic: Not a challenge of modern agriculture
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a challenge facing modern agriculture in India?
options: A) A steady fall in the demand for food
D) Climate change and extreme weather
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) A steady fall in the demand for food
Why: Demand for food keeps rising with population and incomes; it is not falling.
Why not the others: (B) declining soil health, (C) falling water tables and (D) climate change are real challenges.
Key point: Farming must produce more from less land, water and soil health.

questions.topic: Unit 1 (Agrometeorology, Genetics and Plant Breeding, Biochemistry and Microbiology): Seed Science
questions.sub_topic: Seed classes and tag colours — which statement is wrong
questions.question:
Consider the following statements about seed classes in India:
(A) Breeder seed bags carry a golden yellow tag.
(B) Foundation seed bags carry a white tag.
(C) Certified seed bags carry an azure blue tag.
(D) Foundation seed is produced by multiplying certified seed.
Which of the statements given above is NOT correct?
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) (D) only
Why: (D) is false: foundation seed is produced from breeder seed, and certified seed is produced from foundation seed. (A), (B) and (C) give the correct tag colours.
Why not the others: Statements (A), (B) and (C) are all correct.
Key point: Breeder — golden yellow; foundation — white; certified — azure blue.

questions.topic: Unit 1 (Agrometeorology, Genetics and Plant Breeding, Biochemistry and Microbiology): Biochemistry
questions.sub_topic: Biopolymers and their building blocks
questions.question:
Match List-I (Biomolecule) with List-II (Building block).

List-I
(A) Protein
(B) Starch
(C) Nucleic acid
(D) Fat (triglyceride)

List-II
(I) Glucose
(II) Glycerol and fatty acids
(III) Amino acids
(IV) Nucleotides
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) (A)-(III), (B)-(I), (C)-(IV), (D)-(II)
Why: Proteins are built from amino acids (III). Starch is built from glucose (I). Nucleic acids are built from nucleotides (IV). Fats are built from glycerol and fatty acids (II).
Why not the others: Option (A) swaps protein and starch. Option (B) swaps starch and nucleic acid. Option (C) swaps nucleic acid and fat.
Key point: Each biopolymer has its own monomer.

questions.topic: Unit 3 (Crop Production): Crop Production: Introduction and Modern Agriculture
questions.sub_topic: Modern farming approaches and their tools
questions.question:
Match List-I (Approach) with List-II (Example of a tool or practice).

List-I
(A) Precision agriculture
(B) Remote sensing
(C) Conservation agriculture
(D) Natural farming

List-II
(I) Satellite images to estimate crop area
(II) Variable-rate fertilizer application guided by GPS
(III) Beejamrit seed treatment
(IV) Happy Seeder sowing into rice residue without tillage
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) (A)-(II), (B)-(I), (C)-(IV), (D)-(III)
Why: Precision agriculture uses GPS-guided variable-rate application (II). Remote sensing uses satellite images (I). Conservation agriculture uses machines such as the Happy Seeder to sow without tillage into residue (IV). Natural farming uses preparations such as beejamrit (III).
Why not the others: Option (A) swaps precision agriculture and remote sensing. Option (C) swaps remote sensing and conservation agriculture. Option (D) swaps conservation and natural farming.
Key point: Each modern approach has a signature tool.

questions.topic: Unit 2 (Livestock Production): Livestock: Scope, Importance and Breeds
questions.sub_topic: A fine-wool sheep breed
questions.question: Which of the following is an exotic sheep breed famous for fine wool?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Merino
Why: Merino, originally from Spain, produces fine, high-quality wool.
Why not the others: (A) Jamunapari, (C) Barbari and (D) Beetal are Indian goat breeds.
Key point: Merino is the classic fine-wool sheep.

questions.topic: Unit 2 (Livestock Production): Livestock: Scope, Importance and Breeds
questions.sub_topic: Exotic dairy breed with the highest yield
questions.question: Which exotic cattle breed is known for the highest milk yield?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Holstein Friesian
Why: Holstein Friesian, from the Netherlands, gives the highest milk yield of any cattle breed, though its milk is lower in fat.
Why not the others: (A) Jersey gives richer milk but less of it; (B) Brown Swiss and (C) Ayrshire yield less than Holstein Friesian.
Key point: Holstein Friesian — most milk; Jersey — richest milk.

questions.topic: Unit 3 (Crop Production): Weed Control
questions.sub_topic: Critical period of crop–weed competition
questions.question: For most annual field crops, the critical period of crop–weed competition falls:
options: A) in the last week or two before the crop is harvested
B) in the first one-third to one-half of the crop's life
C) only after the crop has flowered and set its grain
D) during storage of the harvested grain in bins
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) in the first one-third to one-half of the crop's life
Why: Weeds do the most damage early, while the crop is establishing. Keeping the field weed-free in the first third to half of the season prevents most of the loss.
Why not the others:
(A) and (C) By then the crop canopy suppresses most weeds.
(D) Weeds do not compete in storage.
Key point: Weed early; the critical period is early in the season.

questions.topic: Unit 3 (Crop Production): Field Crops: Cultivation, Protection and Post-harvest
questions.sub_topic: Crop planted by sets
questions.question: Which crop is planted using 'sets', or stem cuttings with buds?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Sugarcane
Why: Sugarcane is propagated by setts, pieces of stem bearing two or three buds.
Why not the others: (A) pearl millet, (B) groundnut and (C) mustard are sown from seed.
Key point: Sugarcane is planted from setts.

questions.topic: Unit 4 (Horticulture): Horticulture: Importance, Orchards, Gardens and Propagation
questions.sub_topic: Why orchards are irrigated before a frost
questions.question: Why do fruit growers irrigate their orchards when a frosty night is expected?
options: A) Because water dissolves the frost crystals as they form
B) Because irrigation makes the trees go dormant at once
C) Because moist soil stores and releases more heat than dry soil
D) Because wet leaves cannot lose any heat at all
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Because moist soil stores and releases more heat than dry soil
Why: Moist soil conducts and stores heat better and releases it at night, which keeps the air near the ground a little warmer.
Why not the others:
(A) Water does not dissolve frost in this way.
(B) Irrigation does not cause instant dormancy.
(D) Wet leaves still lose heat.
Key point: Light irrigation and smoking protect orchards from frost.

questions.topic: Unit 1 (Agrometeorology, Genetics and Plant Breeding, Biochemistry and Microbiology): Microbiology
questions.sub_topic: Respiration, fermentation and decomposition — which hold
questions.question:
Consider the following statements:
(A) Aerobic respiration releases more energy from each glucose molecule than fermentation does.
(B) Fermentation can take place without oxygen.
(C) Microbes that decompose organic matter release carbon dioxide and plant nutrients.
(D) Decomposition is fastest in cold, dry or waterlogged soils.
Which of the statements given above are correct?
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) (A), (B) and (C) only
Why: (A), (B) and (C) are true. (D) is false: decomposition is fastest in warm, moist, well-aerated soils, and slows in cold, dry or waterlogged conditions.
Why not the others: Options (A), (B) and (C) include the false statement (D).
Key point: Warmth, moisture and air speed up decomposition.

questions.topic: Unit 3 (Crop Production): Soil, Soil Fertility, Fertilizers and Manures
questions.sub_topic: Meaning of soil tilth
questions.question: 'Soil tilth' refers to:
options: A) the total amount of plant nutrients stored in the soil
B) the depth of the water table below the surface of the field
C) the number of earthworms found in one square metre
D) the physical condition of soil for germination and root growth
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) the physical condition of soil for germination and root growth
Why: Tilth describes how well the soil crumbles: its aggregation, porosity and ease of working, which together suit seed germination and root growth.
Why not the others:
(A) That is soil fertility.
(B) The water table is a hydrological feature.
(C) Earthworm count is a biological measure.
Key point: Good tilth = crumbly, well-aerated soil.

questions.topic: Unit 1 (Agrometeorology, Genetics and Plant Breeding, Biochemistry and Microbiology): Genetics and Plant Breeding
questions.sub_topic: Why the semi-dwarf wheats did not lodge
questions.question:
Read the following passage and answer the question that follows.

Hybridization is the crossing of two genetically different plants to bring their good qualities together in one variety. In a self-pollinated crop such as wheat, the breeder first chooses parents that complement each other, for example one with high yield and another with disease resistance. The anthers of the flowers of the female parent are removed before they shed pollen; this is called emasculation. The emasculated spikes are covered with bags so that no stray pollen can reach them. When the stigmas are ready, pollen from the chosen male parent is dusted on them, the spikes are bagged again and labelled. The F₁ plants that grow from the crossed seed are uniform, but in the F₂ generation the genes segregate and the plants vary widely. The breeder selects the best plants in the F₂ and keeps selecting in later generations until the lines breed true. In the 1950s Norman Borlaug and his team in Mexico crossed local wheats with lines carrying dwarfing genes from the Japanese variety Norin 10. The new semi-dwarf wheats had short, stiff straw, so they did not fall over (lodge) when heavily fertilized and irrigated, and they could turn extra nitrogen into grain rather than straw. In the mid-1960s India imported seed of these wheats, and Indian breeders, encouraged by M.S. Swaminathan, selected varieties such as Kalyan Sona and Sonalika from the material. Wheat output rose rapidly, and in 1970 Borlaug received the Nobel Peace Prize for his work against hunger.

Question: According to the passage, why did the new semi-dwarf wheats not lodge under heavy fertilizer and irrigation?
options: A) Their roots grew very deep into the soil.
B) They had short, stiff straw.
C) They were sown at a very low seed rate.
D) They matured before the monsoon arrived.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) They had short, stiff straw.
Why: The passage says the semi-dwarf wheats had short, stiff straw, so they did not fall over when heavily fertilized and irrigated.
Why not the others: (A), (C) and (D) are not given in the passage as the reason.
Key point: Dwarfing genes gave stiff straw and stopped lodging.

questions.topic: Unit 1 (Agrometeorology, Genetics and Plant Breeding, Biochemistry and Microbiology): Genetics and Plant Breeding
questions.sub_topic: Purpose of bagging emasculated spikes
questions.question:

Question: Why, according to the passage, are emasculated spikes covered with bags?
options: A) To keep the spikes warm at night
B) To protect them from birds that eat grain
C) To speed up the ripening of the stigma
D) To stop stray pollen from reaching them
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) To stop stray pollen from reaching them
Why: The passage says the emasculated spikes are bagged so that no stray pollen can reach them.
Why not the others: (A), (B) and (C) are not the reason the passage gives.
Key point: Emasculate to stop selfing; bag to stop stray pollen.

questions.topic: Unit 1 (Agrometeorology, Genetics and Plant Breeding, Biochemistry and Microbiology): Genetics and Plant Breeding
questions.sub_topic: Varieties selected in India from Mexican wheats

Question: Which varieties does the passage say Indian breeders selected from the imported Mexican material?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Kalyan Sona and Sonalika
Why: The passage names Kalyan Sona and Sonalika as varieties selected by Indian breeders.
Why not the others: Norin 10 is the Japanese source of the dwarfing genes, not an Indian selection, and Lerma Rojo is not named in the passage.
Key point: Kalyan Sona and Sonalika were early Indian semi-dwarf wheats.

questions.topic: Unit 1 (Agrometeorology, Genetics and Plant Breeding, Biochemistry and Microbiology): Genetics and Plant Breeding
questions.sub_topic: Why selection continues after the F₂
questions.question:
Read the following passage and answer the question that follows.

Hybridization is the crossing of two genetically different plants to bring their good qualities together in one variety. In a self-pollinated crop such as wheat, the breeder first chooses parents that complement each other, for example one with high yield and another with disease resistance. The anthers of the flowers of the female parent are removed before they shed pollen; this is called emasculation. The emasculated spikes are covered with bags so that no stray pollen can reach them. The breeder selects the best plants in the F₂ and keeps selecting in later generations until the lines breed true. In the mid-1960s India imported seed of these wheats, and Indian breeders, encouraged by M.S. Swaminathan, selected varieties such as Kalyan Sona and Sonalika from the material. Wheat output rose rapidly, and in 1970 Borlaug received the Nobel Peace Prize for his work against hunger.

Question: Based on the passage, why must the breeder keep selecting for several generations after the F₂ before a variety is released?
options: A) Because F₁ plants are always sterile and give no seed
B) Because pollen from the male parent is needed again every generation
C) Because the plants segregate and must be selected until the lines breed true
D) Because dwarfing genes are lost unless the crop is re-crossed to Norin 10
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Because the plants segregate and must be selected until the lines breed true
Why: The passage says genes segregate in the F₂, so plants vary widely. Selection must continue until the lines breed true (become homozygous and uniform).
Why not the others:
(A) The passage says F₁ plants grow and are uniform.
(B) No repeated crossing is described.
(D) No re-crossing to Norin 10 is mentioned.
Key point: Segregation in F₂ means selection until lines breed true.

questions.sub_topic: Statement not supported by the wheat passage

Question: One of the following claims goes beyond what the passage says. Which one?
options: A) The dwarfing genes in Borlaug's wheats came from Norin 10.

C) Semi-dwarf wheats turned extra nitrogen into grain rather than straw.
D) Emasculation is done before the anthers shed pollen.

Why: The passage says Borlaug received the Nobel Peace Prize, not the prize for chemistry.
